title: The Dream of Homeownership Is Haunted by Eviction in This Debut Novel
desc: The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s debut novel, The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus t...
content:
The premise of Andrea Uptmor’s debut novel, The New People, is both gloriously simple and fraught with tension. Newlyweds Emma and Rachel move into a recently foreclosed house in a Midwestern campus town in 2008, but unbeknownst to them, the evicted former owners Charlotte and Dirk are still living in the attic in a form of illicit cohabitation known as phrogging. The contested space of the house—which Charlotte begins to sabotage in the hopes that “the new people” will leave—ultimately grounds the novel’s larger questions about the domestic infrastructure of marriage, homeownership, and parenthood, especially for people whose access to those social institutions has been restricted.  

As a queer millennial who experienced the travails of trying to secure the legal protections of marriage well before the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling, I had no idea how much it would mean to me to encounter a story like this one. Uptmor’s insights into the pressures that both legal and social queerphobia exert on Emma and Rachel’s marriage is pitch-perfect, and I loved the unexpected way in which she intertwines their struggles with those of the much older straight couple. Her approach feels refreshingly nuanced and true to the lived complexities of navigating queer adulthood in a predominantly conservative community. The book frequently made me laugh, and even moved me to tears in public. I should also mention that it is built far more sturdily than the fictional house in question, with well-finished prose and an elegantly constructed plot. In short, it’s a novel I will be thrusting into the hands of queer and straight friends alike in the coming months.

In anticipation of the book’s release, Uptmor and I had a delightful conversation over Zoom this spring about living hauntings and contested domestic spaces, as well as the intersections of queer and economic issues that drew her to revisit 2008 with these particular characters.

Jules Fitz Gerald: I once heard Carmen Maria Machado speak about all stories being haunted house stories, in the sense that they’re haunted both by their writers and by their readers. If you think of yourself as a ghost, what prompted you to haunt this particular fictional house in Indiana?

Andrea Uptmor: This idea of illegally occupying somebody’s home has always been interesting to me. When my wife and I bought our first house in 2013 in South Minneapolis, it was in the middle of a huge rash of foreclosures in the neighborhood, and the day after we moved in, our neighbor was evicted due to foreclosure. Right after he left, a group of squatters moved in and occupied the house. Law enforcement was there all the time with their guns drawn, the windows were broken in, but they couldn’t get these people to leave. It was so fascinating to me, this idea that, for me, home ownership was about a mortgage, and for the people next door, it was about occupying a space. It wasn’t until I learned about phrogging, which is living in somebody’s house without their knowledge—sort of an actual living haunting—that I thought, oh, that’s the story. Because then you’ve got that automatic tension between the people who believe they own the house and the people who are occupying it. 

The house becomes this microcosm of what’s happening in the country.

In terms of why Indiana, that’s a good question. I was living in Iowa at the time that I wrote this and was really feeling what Emma feels throughout the book—not quite belonging, being a woman married to a woman. Like Iowa, Indiana can be one of those on-the-fence places where you just never know, when someone’s cleaning your teeth at the dentist’s office, or giving you an Uber ride, whether they’re a safe person or not. I wanted to recreate that environment for Emma and [the] other characters where there’s this air of uncertainty, where you’re not always sure if people are being intentionally aggressive or bigoted or homophobic, or whether it’s being perceived through Emma’s conditioning. 

JFG: I loved how you handled that in the book. I live very far from Indiana, in rural Oregon, but what you’re describing really resonates. Beyond the place, it was interesting as a reader to look back on that time period, especially as rights that once seemed like legal certainties–like marriage equality–are increasingly in question. What was it like for you to write 2008 from the vantage point of the present?

title: The Catalogue of Lost Things
desc: Every month, our desks at the Review pile up with dozens of soon-to-be published books, only some of which involve writers we have heard of, or subjects we know anything about. More often, we wind up ...
content:
Every month, our desks at the Review pile up with dozens of soon-to-be published books, only some of which involve writers we have heard of, or subjects we know anything about. More often, we wind up with a mix somewhere between that of a cabinet of curiosities and a Little Free Library stocked by an indecisive grad student; this summer, for example, alongside many debut novels and NYRB reissues, we found an Italian chapbook of cat-themed poems from the eighties and a semiepistolary critique of psychiatry whose letters are addressed “Dear Neoliberalism.” While combing through these galleys for good ideas or good writing, I sometimes save passages I like. Here are a few I found in July and August.

—Tarpley Hitt, online editor

 

In our Spring 2024 issue, we published a story by Joanna Kavenna called “The Beautiful Salmon,” about a philosophy student who goes to a dinner party at the house of a “brilliant and terrifying” professor, who has cooked a beautiful salmon. A version of that story appears in Seven: or, How to Play a Game Without Rules (Faber & Faber), Kavenna’s sly and dextrous new novel about the same student and the same professor, who specializes in something called “Box Philosophy,” short for “Thinking outside the Box about Thinking outside the Box.”

At one point, the professor sends the student to Greece to track down a “poet-dentist” named Apostolakis, who is “tangentially linked to Box Philosophy,” but has lately been working on a book he’s calling the Fanouropiton, or the Catalogue of Lost Things: 

The book was divided into short entries, like an encyclopaedia. Things Lost by War. Things Lost by Human Folly. Things Lost Because No One Really Cared About Them. And, Things Lost Because Too Many People Cared About Them—a category full of betrayals and thefts. One entry in Things You’d Assume Were Too Big to Get Lost described an entire galaxy that shone approximately 2.5 million times brighter than the sun, but when various distinguished astronomers gathered to examine it further, they found it had disappeared. No one knew why—they would have needed to find it again to answer the question of why it had vanished.

title: Migration Touches Every Life
desc: Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. In The Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice f...
content:
Valeria Luiselli is no stranger to incorporating tangible records of the world in her writing. In The Story of My Teeth, she exchanged audio recordings with a group of Grupo Jumex workers at a juice factory in Mexico. In Tell Me How It Ends, she listened to, transcribed, and interpreted the testimonies of undocumented children. In Lost Children Archive, the protagonist is a sound documentarist. In Echoes from the Borderlands, Luiselli moved beyond the page to bring the US-Mexico border to life in a 24-hour sonic essay/chapbook that was originally presented as a sound installation. Her newest novel, Beginning Middle End, is written in fragments and includes the sounds of volcanoes exhaling and fishermen singing, among other recordings from Sicily accessible via a QR code in the book.

Beginning Middle End is a mother-daughter road novel that journeys through time and genre. The story unfolds in vignettes as an unnamed narrator and her 12-year-old daughter travel to Sicily to return an archeological relic that the mother’s grandmother had taken years before when she migrated to Mexico. Interspersed polaroid pictures, postcards, and sounds become records of their lives, blurring the boundary of narrative forms as the novel dives into geography, mythology, and archeology. Yet, the beating heart of the story remains these four generations of women, all storytellers in their own way. The narrator/mother is writing her own novel about a mother and daughter on a journey; meanwhile, the daughter is documenting their trip through letters and photographs to her grandmother, whose memory is rapidly failing––archiving memories for the one who is losing them. 

The result: a novel that folds time and writing itself. A tripartite novel with three suitcases, a title in three parts, and a fourth layer nestled inside, like the great-grandmother of the stolen relic and the memories the characters in Beginning Middle End are trying to piece together. The story leaves the reader wondering how fractured memories can be preserved and told through fabricated narratives. What is it to live in the middle when memories are fading away?

Valeria Luiselli and I are both Mexican writers, born on the same day of the same year, both living in the United States. Via Zoom, we talked about sounds, migration, tectonic plates, translation, and the power of fiction and narrative to shape children’s imaginations. 

Ofelia Montelongo: As I was reading the novel, I kept thinking about how themes of displacement and the mother-daughter relationship have been central to your earlier work. How did your earlier work migrate into the imagination of this novel?

There’s always a moment in a novel when you have to abandon a path because you are already on another. Those abandoned paths are ones that I often pick up again in another book.

Valeria Luiselli: There is a line of continuity in many of my books. Maybe not a line that traverses all of them. I certainly see a very clear line from Los ingrávidos or Faces in the Crowd (2011), through this tiny thing I wrote that very few people have read called Swings of Harlem––a map of swings in Harlem where I started using Polaroid photography for the first time while documenting, in that case, a neighborhood and the swings in the neighborhood. And then, from Swings Of Harlem to Lost Children Archive and, of course, Tell Me How it Ends as well, but that’s a very straightforward, nonfictional testimonial piece.

OM: How are the narrators and main characters different in each story? And different from you as the author?

title: 3 Debut Authors Discuss How to Live in the Hypothetical
desc: For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One ma...
content:
For the spring edition of our debut craft series, three debut authors—Alexa Yasemin Brahme, Sonia Feldman, and Vincent Yu—discuss in detail their journeys through writing about imaginary lives. One may argue that all fiction is rooted in imaginary lives, but these novels especially feel centered around the stakes of these imaginary lives as the protagonists confront, examine, wonder, and muse upon each of their choice’s ramifications on the rest of their years. From the gritty-and-glamorous art scene of Manhattan to the humid teenage June of northeastern Ohio to a suburban, emergency-laden town in Massachusetts, these three novels feature forks in the road and irreversible decisions that fall like dominoes upon characters and their next chapters. 

“It was strange to see John in the studio, completely at a loss as to how to move his body, unsure of how to orient himself toward art.” So begins Good News by Alexa Yasemin Brahme, a novel centered on Maggie, a Turkish-American MFA student finalizing her evocative thesis painting of “feminine suffering” while competing with her brother’s girlfriend, who has given herself the moniker of “the Artist.” Set in the contemporary New York art scene, the novel follows Maggie as she tries to orient herself within a branching future. Through gallery openings, social climbing parties, doubts about her boyfriend, and the return of an enigmatic ex, Maggie is forced to decide which life or alternate life she’ll end up choosing. In this world, a vertical brushstroke can change the entire canvas, and one phone call can upend everything she’s built. Good News invites it all, plus the chaos, pleasure, and temptation of being young—that is, of creating worlds that leak out of our heads. 

“Growing up, I had two best friends—Margaret, whom I had known my whole life, and Eleanor, with whom I was in love, though for years I had no reason to tell my feelings for one apart from my feelings for the other.” In Girl’s Girl by Sonia Feldman—set in that long summer between freshman and sophomore year of high school—Mina is caught in a web of desire, both platonic and erotic. It is a novel about living in suburban Ohio and creating those “capital E Experiences” that stay with you long after graduation. Reading it, I could almost smell the chlorine of untouched pools and that sticky perfume of bug spray sweating off skin at the end of the night. The messiness of the Midwest summer and unrequited love and dazzling adolescent confessions run rampant in this debut. 

 

“Beckitt’s emergency began on a calm spring morning: an expansive chill in the air; the sun soaring over rangy, adolescent clouds; miles of rolling green mowed into submission, flanked by grand columns of oak and maple, through which the wind shivered.” When a ballistic missile alert threatens the town of Beckitt on a mundane morning, the town and its cast of characters are confronted with that most human decision: fight-or-flight. But when the second alert comes in, claiming that the first was a false alarm, the real decisions become clear. Where does one go from here? What did each person choose to save or leave behind? And how will these ramifications infiltrate the rest of their lives and those surrounding them? Seek Immediate Shelter by Vincent Yu explores the question of “what if” at its zenith. The novel follows five different characters and moves through each of their perspectives when the alert was sent, and then the aftermath, which for some may prove to be an even more daunting emergency than that initial missile threat. 

Brahme, Feldman, and Yu corresponded with me on the significance of perspective in their novels, the spark that ignited and transformed their hypothetical questions into fiction, and the advice they would impart to anyone becoming a debut novelist. 

Kyla D Walker: Did you know right away that the book would be from Maggie’s third-person limited POV, or did you consider a first-person POV as well? What ultimately led you to choose third-person narration, and how did this change the novel’s approach?

Alexa Yasemin Brahme: First person is an intimidating point of view—“I” can be very powerful. First person felt immediate, intimate, and had a sure-footedness that wasn’t quite right for Maggie. The first person feels to me like certainty. We readers are getting the account straight from the source, and when that source is unreliable, like I think Maggie would be, the first person feels like a slight of hand a character is performing against the reader. What’s presented as fact is actually distorted. I wanted there to be a little distance between the reader and Maggie so she couldn’t hide from their gaze. Maggie can’t present her take on the situation because the reader can see multiple sides at once. While Maggie can trick herself into believing one version of the story, she can’t trick the reader.

title: Finding Your Voice as a Woman Writer Raised on Books by Men
desc: Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently ...
content:
Julie Buntin and I first met when Electric Literature shared an office with Catapult in the mid-2010s. She was a book editor and the director of Catapult’s beloved educational program; I had recently become Electric Literature’s Executive Director. I was an aspiring writer with a few short stories; Julie was about to publish her debut novel, Marlena, to critical and commercial acclaim. We hit it off as two hard-working, mostly type-A people with the same cynical sense of humor that protects over-eager emotions, and began trading work after we both left the city. Julie to Ann Arbor where she was teaching at the University of Michigan and writing her sophomore novel, Famous Men; me to upstate New York where I was working on my debut novel, Slush, which will be published next summer. Julie is my most trusted reader. I have long felt like I can say anything to her; that nothing is too strange, or dark, or vulnerable, or naïve. If I am working out a difficult opinion, she can help me articulate it. What better qualities to have in a writing partner?

Famous Men tells the story of Wilhelmina Miles, known as Will, an aspiring poet from the small town of Greening, Michigan. She has long harbored the fantasy that her town’s one success story, the decorated writer Nathanial Fellow, is her father. When she moves to New York and tracks him down at the MFA program where he teaches, that fantasy deforms into a relationship, one that is financial, professional, sexual, and even a little familial.

Famous Men is an entertaining, rich, discomfiting novel that rejects black and white answers to complex questions in favor of subjectivity as its foundational stance. Consent is not a matter of “yes” or “no,” culpability is not an easy verdict, and power is multi-directional.

Reading early drafts of Famous Men, I was struck by how they never quite felt like drafts. Scenes were cut, plot points changed, etc., but the world of the novel and the ideas behind it always felt fully formed. Julie has a charismatic prose style that is flowing yet precise, with a clarity of insight that seems casual but is most certainly hard won. When the galley finally arrived, I thought I would dip in and out to gather questions for this interview. But I couldn’t resist reading straight through for a third time; the novel is that compelling and rewarding.

Julie and I spoke over video call, with some follow-up over email. I found myself surprisingly nervous to ask her “serious questions” on the record, after so many casual, private conversations. Initial giggling aside, we settled in, and I was grateful to be able to engage with her not as my friend, but as the author of one of my favorite books of this decade.

Halimah Marcus: Will, long before she ever meets Nathaniel, reads his work at the library. And because they’re from the same small town, it sparks her imagination about what she could be someday. Who were the writers that did that for you when you were that age?

Julie Buntin: I grew up in Hemingway country. I grew up in the Petoskey area of Northern Michigan where the Nick Adams stories on Walloon Lake are set. Hemingway lived in a lot of places, but there’s a lot of regional Hemingway pride where I’m from in a way I took for granted as a young person—that a small town like that might celebrate their literary grandfather out of pride. My husband’s family is from Lorain, Ohio, where Toni Morrison is from, and he went looking for her house once. There was nothing that said Toni Morrison lived there.

Hemingway was a writer I liked and read at a young age because we had his books in our house, The Sun Also Rises, For Whom the Bell Tolls, obviously the stories. I wasn’t necessarily thinking, I want to write like this, but I did have this idea of certain writers as having this cultural impact. I also read a ton of Stephen King, like so much Stephen King.

title: James Joyce’s Baby Impressions and Other “Awkward Pleasures” of Literary Biography
desc: In the Lake District, 1994.Each week, The Paris Review unlocks stories, poems, and interviews for our readers from our archive. This week, we’ve unlocked our interview with Hermione Lee, selected from...
content:
In the Lake District, 1994.

Each week, The Paris Review unlocks stories, poems, and interviews for our readers from our archive. This week, we’ve unlocked our interview with Hermione Lee, selected from the archive by Daisy Hildyard, whose story “Two Lives” appears in our recent Summer issue. Sign up for the Redux newsletter to receive these pieces to your inbox every Sunday morning.

Everybody dabbles in biography. If you have ever spoken at a funeral, rewritten your CV, or gossiped, you’ve had to deal with some of the questions that Hermione Lee discusses with Louisa Thomas in her Art of Biography interview. What is the shape of a life? What are the ingredients of an achievement? What specific person and what particular circumstances produced it? When something fails, do we have to find somebody to blame? Lee addresses these questions as matters of technique: the work of finding, or inventing, “a structure that is sympathetic to the subject.”

There is a kind of mise en abyme at play in her work, and in this interview about the life of somebody who writes the lives of those who captured something of life in their writing. Literary biography is an awkward pleasure. I like its strange textures and surprises. You catch James Joyce doing his impressions of a baby, or spend the summer with Tolstoy when he is on one of his horse yogurt diets. I believed I had a fair understanding of W. G. Sebald until I read his biography and saw the black-and-white snapshot of him as a young man standing thigh-deep in a river, topless in wet jeans with a deep tan, defined muscles, and a dagger in his hand. I also enjoy the genre for its practical insights. It’s useful to know how other writers chased their invoices, or when their children napped.

Lee’s biographies are exceptional for their integration of original research with illuminating interpretations of the authors’ works, and they last. I’ve read and reread her Penelope Fitzgerald and Virginia Woolf; I’ve used the footnotes and followed her sources. I still have my mother’s twenty-nine-year-old Virago Press paperback Willa Cather. I can’t think of another writer, biographer or otherwise, who reads as closely as Lee, or with the same balance and imagination.

In their searching conversation, I was particularly interested in what Lee and Thomas have to say about the undisclosed elements of a life, including Lee’s own (she is reticent). They discuss lies and secrets. They also discuss inventiveness and hard work. The interview leaves me with a sense of how much it takes to make a sincere attempt to understand another person’s life.

 

The Art of Biography No. 4 Hermione Lee, interviewed by Louisa Thomas

title: If You Build It, Will They Come? On the Sperm Racing World Cup
desc: Ghadeer Bustani, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.In 1677, a medical student named Johann Ham approached the Dutch scientist and future “Father of Microbiology” Antonie van Leeuwenhoek with unsettl...
content:
Ghadeer Bustani, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

In 1677, a medical student named Johann Ham approached the Dutch scientist and future “Father of Microbiology” Antonie van Leeuwenhoek with unsettling news: there were tiny creatures living in his semen. Or not in his semen, not necessarily. Some incorrigible friend—someone who certainly wasn’t Ham—had dislodged his wad in the company of an “unclean woman” and then transferred custody of his deposit by means unattested into Ham’s hands. Curious Ham had splashed the discharge under a microscope and, startled by its contents, brought his discovery and its medium to Van Leeuwenhoek for a second opinion. Examining the sample, the renowned microscopist, who had already described what we call red blood cells and protists in pioneering detail, glimpsed spindly tailed animalcules moving in the muck. He proceeded to set about procuring new goo from a close, morally uncompromised source. “What I here describe was not obtained by any sinful contrivance on my part, but the observations were made upon the excess with which Nature provided me in my conjugal relations,” he wrote some months later to the Royal Society of London regarding the remains of an emission he’d slathered under his powerful single-lens microscope. 

I relate this lightly editorialized and moderately abridged history of the identification of what would become known as spermatozoa because it marks the first time that a man had cause and the capability to wonder at the meaning of the living contents of his ejaculate—and thus to search his little reflecting pool for the secrets of humanity, of himself. And because, in 2024, some 347 years after Van Leeuwenhoek fired his fateful blast, a money-minded form of this fascination prompted a team of teenage and early-twenties shitpost entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley to found a sports start-up called Sperm Racing. It has raised $10 million in funding.

The company first came to my attention this February, a month before it was due to roll out an ambitious Sperm Racing World Cup featuring contestants representing 128 countries. When an editor for this magazine asked me to write about the championship, I began to picture myself as an anxious, anthropomorphized gamete paddling desperately toward its subject, its theme, its egg, endeavoring to fulfill its purpose, to conceive a story. Come is, as it happens, a subject on which I enjoy some expertise. Through the power of the internet and promiscuity, I’ve learned to appreciate the rich diversity of whitish matter the human body can produce. Color, velocity, viscosity, volume, reach, and duration differ from person to person, from shot to shot. I’ve become familiar with the venerable tradition, staged between men (and not only men) every day, of exhibition, comparison, and analysis, in which the relation between the two parties, or between one’s fantasy and one’s reality, or between one’s present output and one’s memory of past productions, adds to the pleasure that inheres in the act itself. 

Sperm Racing is, more or less, a scientized and de-eroticized update on this “venerable tradition.” At the Sperm Racing headquarters in San Francisco, two contestants donate their semen, which is centrifugally cleaned; healthy sperm are isolated from the samples; and the cells then race through courses less than a half-centimeter long that are etched into microfluidic silicon chips. The sperm are pipetted into warm liquid currents designed to mimic the reproductive environment; these currents allow the cells to orient themselves in the faux canal, such that the cells begin to swim upstream, as they would against the flow of mucus in a vagina, toward the finish line. (Until recently, the company’s chief science officer was a teenager named Rishi Kanaparti, whose past work includes papers on, among other things, “Motion Resilient Deep Learning for ECG Signal Classification.”) The raw footage is boring and difficult for the human eye to parse—vaguely defined blobs move against a white background—so the company’s computers track the cells’ coordinates and generate visual approximations of the contests. They then debut these videos at occasional live events, like one that pitted a USC student against a UCLA student last April, and post them on social media. Several Reels on Instagram feature a bellowing commentator who goes by BSTCHLD. “This is a microscopic masterclass,” BSTCHLD shouts during one blowout. As a sperm enters the end zone: “INSEMINATION!”

In preparing for the World Cup, I imagined how I might engage my subject. I could follow the matches as they unfolded. I would attend a race if possible; I might host a watch party; I might gather some gays at my house to shoot rope on camera for an unaffiliated competition during the watch party. Sperm Racing could beget fagslop. I had thoughts. I had plans. They would, at length, go somewhat bust. 

***

One such plan: In the spirit of participatory journalism, I applied to the Sperm Racing World Cup a few days after receiving this assignment, assuming that I would be screened out for being old (thirty-three), common (American), and of no particular repute as a content creator and thus of no particular value to a would-be sport whose founders require significant reserves of the public’s attention for their goop regatta saga to succeed. I answered questions about my ancestry, diet, workout frequency and routine, and motivations (options included “fertility awareness” and “national pride”). I dutifully took screenshots of the Sperm Racing webpage and forwarded them to my editor. I scoured my inbox for a form email explaining my unworthiness—“Do Not Come,” its subject line might have read—but found nothing. I waited.

title: In the Studio with Chad Fore, the Writer Behind “Lil Spooky”
desc: Photograph by Kathleen McNamara.In the time between his first submission to the Review, in February of last year, and the publication of his short story “Lil Spooky” in our new Summer issue, the write...
content:
Photograph by Kathleen McNamara.

In the time between his first submission to the Review, in February of last year, and the publication of his short story “Lil Spooky” in our new Summer issue, the writer Chad Fore and I exchanged almost a hundred emails. I also read several of his stories, which tend to be somewhat autobiographical, at least in the sense that they often take place in one of Fore’s two neighboring hometowns—Piru and Fillmore, in Southern California—and are rich with the kinds of details and characters that feel impossible to invent. “Lil Spooky” follows its high-school-age protagonist, Brad Camacho, through his gradual—then all too fast—initiation into a local gang. In a humiliation ritual disguised as a tryout, he has to freestyle for members of the gang’s hip-hop arm, also known as the Sick Minded Clique, which records posse cuts in a “decrepit old shack” they call the studio, at the end of one of their driveways. Knowing what I did about Fore’s fiction, I wasn’t entirely surprised when, alongside the first draft of this story, he included the link to a song he was featured on when he himself was in high school. He and I talked about the musical influences of his characters and of his own past over lunch this spring, when, after all those messages, we were finally able to meet in person. I found he has an encyclopedic memory for rap verses, some by artists we both love, and others that he’s been writing in his head, he said, for twenty years. 

 

INTERVIEWER 

While we were editing “Lil Spooky,” you told me it was partly inspired by time you spent with your older cousin’s rap group in the nineties and early aughts. What drew you to that specific experience as a subject and how did you approach writing about it after so many years? 

CHAD FORE

From the start I had in mind the type of story I wanted to write. When I think of friends from my hometown or family members who got involved in gangs or drugs or whatever—there were always opportunities before it got bad, where they could still get out of it. But then something happens, and they can’t anymore. I wanted the story to end at that moment where, without having been told anything, the reader would know that Brad’s in a different place, and now it is too late. There was one sentence that I almost cut. I went back and forth. Does this explain too much? Does it not explain enough? 

INTERVIEWER
